prize_parts.citation: for developing targeted protein degradation by chemically induced proximity, through PROTAC degraders and the molecular basis of thalidomide-type molecular glues

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation is the clearest case on the list of a molecular design principle that changed what chemists and clinicians can do. Heterobifunctional molecules and molecular glues turn the ubiquitin-proteasome system into a programmable chemical reaction, remove rather than inhibit a target, and make proteins without a conventional binding pocket tractable. It is the best-supported lead in the openings: three first-place votes and four top-three placements. Five of eight members ranked it in the top four, and it spans chemical biology, medicinal chemistry and structural biology. Crews and Deshaies supplied the PROTAC concept and its first demonstrations, and Handa identified cereblon as the thalidomide target, which explains the glue arm and the clinical immunomodulatory drug story.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that eight credited names sit under one heading and only three can be honoured, so Ciulli (VHL ligands, rational design), Sakamoto (first PROTAC) and Gray are left out. PROTACs and glues may also be two separate discoveries. In addition, clinical validation is still emerging: as far as I know no degrader is approved, and I could not verify that from the files. If the committee wants a completed clinical record, recognition could be slightly early.

responses.point: Somfai asks what is new chemically in degraders, notes there is no approved PROTAC yet, and sees recognition as possibly premature.
responses.response: I take the maturity point seriously, but I think the chemical novelty is real. The design principle is that a bifunctional molecule creates a neo-interaction, so cooperative ternary complex formation and linker and ligand optimisation become the chemistry, and molecular glues show that a small molecule can reshape a protein surface to recruit a new substrate. That differs from classic occupancy-driven inhibition. For me the test is replication and the change in practice, and both are met: many independent labs and industry programmes work on it, and the field has reshaped how drug discovery is done. Approval is a useful signal but not the criterion for a chemistry prize.

responses.point: Linke ranks degraders fourth and flags that the ternary-complex biophysics is only partly quantified, that Handa and Ito's cereblon work is a distinct strand, and that no approvals are firm, so recognition may be slightly early.
responses.response: I agree the cooperativity biophysics is not yet fully quantitative, but that is a reason the field is generative rather than a reason to wait. On the distinct strand, I would keep Handa in because cereblon explains why thalidomide-type drugs work and links the glue story to the PROTAC story through the same E3-ligase hijacking logic. Under a three-person cap that is a framing choice, not a claim that Ciulli and Sakamoto matter less. If Linke or others want to split the strands into two prize parts, I would be open to hearing that, but I would not give up the unified citation lightly.

responses.point: Aqvist puts degraders first and anchors on Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, treating the glue arm as a competing credit stream that cannot fit in three.
responses.response: I share his top ranking and his view that the crowded credit is the main weakness. Where I differ is on the third name. Ciulli's VHL ligands made rational design and structural mechanism possible, and that is a strong claim. But Handa's cereblon identification is what makes the thalidomide mechanism and the largest clinical class of degraders intelligible, so the prize would otherwise omit an entire half of the field. I would like to hear a structural argument that the PROTAC arm alone is the cleaner story.

responses.point: Sparr ranks ionizable lipid nanoparticles first, on lipid self-assembly physical chemistry and global validation, noting a split between Vancouver and Boston credit and overlap with the 2023 Medicine prize.
responses.response: Her case for lipid nanoparticles is a strong one: the validation is enormous and the self-assembly chemistry is a real design principle. My reservation is attribution, since Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer all have claims that a three-person cap cannot separate cleanly. I also think the downstream mRNA impact is partly carried by the 2023 Medicine prize. I therefore keep it as an alternative and would support it if the discussion shows a clean three-name attribution.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers a PROTAC-focused trio (with Ciulli) or a PROTAC-plus-cereblon trio (with Handa), or two prize parts.
Clinical approval status of degraders, which is from my memory and not verified in the provided files.
Whether prior recognition in adjacent areas (2023 Medicine, 2020 Chemistry CRISPR) lowers the appetite for delivery or genome-editing prizes.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My research interest in peptide and nanoparticle biosensing, and my link to Emma Sparr through self-assembly work, do not bear on the degrader or the lipid nanoparticle candidates. I have no known ties to the credited names.
